query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A high-throughput DSC/DTA protocol can accurately determine the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume change at melting for equiatomic high-entropy alloys within 5% error compared to conventional measurements.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic single-phase HEA samples (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) prepared by arc melting and subsequently processed into powders.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to a high-throughput DSC/DTA measurement using miniaturized, calibrated crucibles (e.g., alumina with ceramic liners), under a dual-atmosphere protocol (nitrogen for lower temperatures and inert argon for high temperatures) with controlled heating rates (≈10 K/min).
generation.conditions: Temperature ramp from room temperature up to above melting (up to ~1600 °C) with careful baseline corrections and multiple cycles to ensure reproducibility.
generation.structural_mediator: The onset of melting marked by abrupt endothermic peaks, rapid enthalpy changes, and associated volumetric expansion deduced from simultaneous thermal analysis.
generation.mechanism: The controlled heating allows precise detection of latent heat absorption and onset of atomic rearrangements during melting, following known thermal kinetic principles (Debye and Dulong–Petit behavior).
generation.predicted_outcome: Fusion enthalpy and melting temperature will be measured with an uncertainty of ±5% and ±10 K, respectively, relative to conventional DSC baseline values.
generation.baseline: Traditional DSC measurements reported in literature (e.g., PMC7513177 and PMC11642357) using slower, conventional protocols.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable to HEAs with melting points below ~1600 °C where crucible reactivity and oxidation are minimized.
generation.uncertainty: Measurement uncertainties are expected to be below ±5% for enthalpy values and ±10 K for melting temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform parallel DSC/DTA experiments on a set of HEA samples using both the high-throughput protocol and a conventional DSC protocol.
measurements: Melting temperature as determined by the onset of endothermic peaks
Fusion enthalpy through integration over the endothermic events
Volume change via concurrent dilatometry if available
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-throughput measurements deviate by more than ±10% from the conventional DSC baseline values, then the hypothesis and the proposed protocol are falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 1 presents the DSC analysis results for the Mn16Cr16Ni16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy during heating and cooling. During heating (red curve), two distinct endothermic peaks are observed. The first peak starts at 1113.7 K, reaches a maximum at 1201.7 K, and ends at 1228.1 K, with an absorbed energy of −10.1 J/g. The second, more intense endothermic peak begins at 1297.7 K and ends at 1327.2 K, corresponding to the melting process, with an energy absorption of −70.53 J/g. During cooling (blue curve), two exothermic peaks appear, indicating crystallization processes. The first peak starts at 1126.6 K, reaches a maximum at 1154.0 K, and ends at 1198.9 K, with a released energy of −9.1 J/g. The second, more pronounced exothermic peak begins at 1198.9 K, reaches a maximum at 1297.2 K, and ends at 1305.9 K, releasing −48.3 J/g, suggesting the crystallization of the primary phase from the liquid.

The calculation of configurational entropy, also called mixing entropy, is given in Equation (3) with n as the number of elements, xi the concentration of each element i and R as the universal gas constant. The equation is derived from the mixing of noble gases and is adopted to fully disordered solid solution, which are assumed in our work. If elements are distributed non-equally between possible sub-lattices, then a more general equation should be used []. In case of an equiatomic alloy, Equation (3) is reduced to ΔSconf=Rlnn. Thus the configurational entropy of 5-component equiatomic alloy is ~1.6·R. At 0 K the resulting total entropy may not be zero. This does not violate the third law of thermodynamics (dSdT|T=0=0) which is often misinterpreted as S(T = 0) = 0. Crystalline solids may exhibit a non-zero entropy at the absolute zero point due to a randomly crystallographic orientation. A change of entropy in this point is not possible, because there is no ability of motion or diffusion. papers.title: How atoms of polycrystalline Nb20.6Mo21.7Ta15.6W21.1V21.0 refractory high entropy alloys rearra
papers.system: Refractory high-entropy alloys (Nb–Mo–Ta–W–V) in both single crystal and polycrystalline forms
papers.approach: Large-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using a 2NN MEAM potential combined with MaxEnt generated structures; investigation of density profiles and enthalpy curves during controlled heating
papers.findings: For the single crystal, an abrupt density drop from 11.25 to 11.00 g/cm³ in the temperature range 2910 to 2940 K indicated the onset of collective local structural rearrangement. For polycrystalline samples, a two-stage melting process was observed: pre-melting at grain boundaries followed by bulk melting at the system melting point, with an empirical relation found linking grain size and melting point.
papers.mechanism: Melting proceeds via a two-stage process with grain-boundary pre-melting initiating local atomic rearrangements, followed by a collective, bulk rearrangement marked by changes in chemical short-range order.

papers.title: Entropy Determination of Single-Phase High Entropy Alloys with Different Crystal Structures over a Wide Temperature Range.
papers.system: Single-phase high-entropy alloys (various crystal structures: fcc, bcc, and hcp) and single-crystalline nickel
papers.approach: Experimental determination of temperature-dependent molar heat capacity cp(T) using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) over a wide temperature range (from −170 °C up to the solidus temperature); calorimetric and mixing entropy calculations
papers.findings: Thermal entropy values calculated from integrated cp(T) data were found to be nearly equal across alloys with the same crystal structure. The configurational entropy (determined via mixing rules, e.g., ΔSconf = R ln(n)) provided a vertical offset in total entropy but played a lesser role in absolute values compared to thermal entropy.
papers.mechanism: The physical rationale is that Cp values follow the Debye T³ law at low temperatures and approach 3R (Dulong–Petit law) at higher temperatures, with the measured cp data capturing solely the thermal vibrational contributions, while the configurational part remains as an offset.

papers.title: Computational property predictions of Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr high-entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Hybrid Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics (MC/MD) simulations performed with thousands of atoms to evolve structures and calculate thermodynamic quantities (ΔH, ΔS, ΔG) during annealing at high temperatures (e.g., 1800 °C)
papers.findings: The simulations showed that initial thermodynamic evolution is driven mainly by enthalpy changes, transitioning to significant configurational entropy contributions as MC swaps progress. Convergence of ΔG within a few percent was achieved after about 30–40 MC swaps, indicating close approach to thermodynamic equilibrium.
papers.mechanism: Local chemical clustering and deviations from ideal random solution behavior contribute to significant configurational entropy effects, which influence the free energy landscape of the alloy; the interplay of enthalpic and entropic contributions dictates phase stability.

papers.title: Thermal Analysis of High-Entropy Rare Earth Oxides.
papers.system: High-entropy rare earth sesquioxides (RE2O3 systems with equimolar ratios, e.g., La, Sm, Dy, Er, and Nd/Gd/Y)
papers.approach: A combination of splat quenching from the melt, high-temperature differential thermal analysis (DTA), synchrotron X-ray diffraction, and CALPHAD modeling to measure melting points, enthalpy of fusion, and volume changes at melting
papers.findings: Three reversible high-temperature phase transitions were identified (assigned as transformations into A, H, and X structure types). The melting point of one composition was determined as 2456 ± 12 °C, which was higher than any of the constituent oxides, suggesting the influence of nonideal mixing.
papers.mechanism: The enhanced melting temperature is attributed to non-ideal mixing in both the solid and liquid states, along with volume change observations during phase transitions that align with known tendencies in pure rare earth systems.

papers.title: Thermal and Structural Analysis of a High-Entropy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 Alloy-Infl
papers.approach: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurements during controlled heating and cooling cycles to capture melting and crystallization endo-/exothermic events, combined with complementary structural characterization (XRD, SEM, TEM)
papers.findings: Two distinct endothermic peaks during heating were attributed to initial phase changes and subsequent melting; corresponding exothermic peaks appeared during cooling indicating crystallization. The melting process was identified by a large endothermic peak with quantifiable energy absorption.
papers.mechanism: The detected thermal events reflect energy absorption during melting (fusion enthalpy) and the associated entropy changes, linked to the breaking and rearrangement of atomic bonds in the complex, multicomponent alloy.

papers.title: Microstructure and Thermal Analysis of Metastable Intermetallic Phases in High-Entropy Alloy CoCrFeMo0.85Ni.
papers.approach: Use of differential thermal analysis (DTA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine phase transition temperatures (including solidus, liquidus, and intermetallic formation/dissolution), with accompanying microstructural (SEM, EDX) characterization
papers.findings: Distinct transition temperatures were identified: phase transitions at around 800 °C (intermetallic formation) and 1212 °C, with solidus and liquidus temperatures of approximately 1323 °C and 1331 °C. CALPHAD predictions provided a phase diagram that was compared with thermal measurements.
papers.mechanism: Thermal transitions are driven by eutectic reactions and the interplay between intermetallic phase formation and dissolution, demonstrating how local composition modulations impact the melting behavior and latent heat characteristics.

papers.title: Third-Generation Thermodynamic Descriptions for Ta-Cr and Ta-V Binary Systems.
papers.system: Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems (pure element and intermetallic phases in both solid A2 and liquid states)
papers.approach: Development of third-generation Gibbs energy models using a two-state model to separately calculate the contributions of enthalpy, entropy, heat capacity, and thermal vacancy effects, validated by comparisons with experimental Cp and enthalpy data
papers.findings: The new Gibbs energy expressions accurately capture the thermodynamic properties down to 0 K, including thermal vacancy concentrations near the melting point, and show excellent agreement with measured data across the temperature range up to 6000 K.
papers.mechanism: A combination of theoretical modeling and semi-empirical corrections allows a consistent description of both the solid and liquid phases, successfully linking heat capacity behavior to the fundamental thermodynamic parameters (H, S, Cp) relevant for melting and liquid-phase properties.

established: DSC/DTA experiments can reliably measure specific heat, latent heat, and transition temperatures (solidus/liquidus) in high-entropy alloys.
MD and MC/MD simulations capture local atomic rearrangements and can elucidate multi-stage melting processes, including grain-boundary effects.
CALPHAD modeling, supported by experimental phase diagram data, is effective for predicting phase equilibria and thermodynamic properties in multicomponent systems.

approaches_tried.approach: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulation with advanced potentials (e.g., 2NN MEAM)
approaches_tried.outcome: Elucidated melting mechanisms through density and enthalpy profiles; demonstrated grain-size influences and multi-stage melting but requires extensive computational resources and careful potential validation.

approaches_tried.approach: Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) and Differential Thermal Analysis (DTA) measurements
approaches_tried.outcome: Successfully determined melting temperatures, fusion enthalpy, and entropy contributions for various HEA systems, albeit with challenges in deconvoluting overlapping transitions and effects from rapid solidification.
Offered insights into equilibrium thermodynamics (ΔH, ΔS, ΔG) during high-temperature annealing with reasonable convergence criteria, highlighting the importance of configurational contributions.

approaches_tried.approach: CALPHAD Modeling combined with first-principles and empirical data
approaches_tried.outcome: Provided phase diagram predictions and estimates of fusion enthalpy and lattice stability; accuracy hinges on underlying database quality and empirical calibration.

mechanisms: Local structural rearrangements at the atomic scale, including collective behavior during melting.
Grain boundary pre-melting that initiates the melting process ahead of bulk melting.
Configurational entropy due to chemical clustering and deviations from ideal randomness contributes significantly to free energy changes at high temperatures.
Non-ideal mixing effects in both solid and liquid phases, which impact melting temperature and fusion properties.
disagreements: Differences in quantifying the relative roles of thermal versus configurational entropy in stabilizing the solid-solution phase across different measurement techniques.
Variations between CALPHAD predictions and experimental DSC/DTA results in terms of exact phase transition temperatures and intermetallic formation sequences.
The challenge in accurately modeling fusion enthalpy for intermetallic compounds compared to Hmix used as a proxy, leading to uncertainty in absolute thermodynamic values.
open_questions: How to generalize and calibrate these experimental and simulation methods to cover the vast compositional space of HEAs with uniformly high accuracy?
What is the optimal integration of MD/MC simulations with experimental measurements (DSC, DTA, neutron imaging) to decouple configurational and thermal contributions across different HEA families?
How do liquid-phase properties (such as viscosity and thermal conductivity) connect quantitatively with the measured fusion parameters, and can these be modeled with similar efficiency?
opportunities: Combining high-throughput CALPHAD assessments with targeted DSC/DTA experiments and advanced MD/MC simulations can provide a more comprehensive mapping of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume changes.
Integrating in-situ techniques (e.g., neutron imaging) with rapid heating/cooling experiments may yield decisive validation results by directly visualizing liquid-phase behavior and mixing.
Developing hybrid simulation–experimental frameworks that utilize machine learning to extrapolate parameters across compositions could significantly improve efficiency and predictive accuracy.

Future work could focus on establishing a definitive benchmark where discrepancies between simulation and experiment (e.g., mispredicted melting temperatures or latent heats) would rule out an inadequate theoretical approach.

directions.assessment: Developing a high-throughput DSC/DTA protocol using miniaturized, well‐calibrated sample holders and dual-atmosphere setups directly targets accurate measurements of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume changes. The physics (thermal events, latent heat absorption) have long been used to assess fusion properties in HEAs (see PMC7513177 and PMC11642357). This approach is directly aligned with the measurement challenges and is feasible if overlapping transitions are deconvoluted effectively.

directions.direction: In-Situ Neutron Imaging with Rapid Heating
directions.assessment: By combining high-temperature in-situ neutron imaging with controlled heating, one can directly visualize liquid-phase behaviors (e.g., mixing/demixing and volume expansion) that determine liquid-phase thermodynamic properties. The rationale is based on imaging the spatial evolution of the melt (see PMC8320920), with quantitative spatial and temperature resolution. The method is directly relevant for properties that are otherwise inferred from calorimetry.

Hybrid Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics simulation approaches can capture both enthalpic and configurational contributions during melting, accurately predicting melting temperatures and fusion thermodynamics. The physical basis and convergence criteria (e.g., <2.5% ΔG differences) are supported by studies (PMC7921137), making this a promising and computationally efficient route to screen large parts of the HEA compositional space.

Integrating high-throughput CALPHAD assessments with machine learning models can extrapolate and predict thermodynamic fusion parameters across vast compositional spaces. The physical rationale is to combine validated thermodynamic databases (see PMC7412006 and PMC8950179) with ML to improve efficiency and accuracy. Key uncertainties lie in training data quality but the approach can be a breakthrough if successfully validated.

directions.direction: Laser Melting and Aerodynamic Levitation with Synchrotron X-Ray Diffraction
directions.assessment: Using laser melting in combination with aerodynamic levitation and real-time synchrotron X-ray diffraction can capture rapid melting behaviors, volume changes, and liquid-phase structure. While powerful, this approach is complex and equipment-intensive. It is a more direct method for highly refractory or off-stoichiometric HEAs where conventional crucible methods risk contamination.
